note: AI terms & acronyms for the Definitions search. Authored by category and adversarially fact-checked (skeptic pass corrected/flagged defs); the updater can add new terms.

terms.def: Data-center power design delivering 800-volt direct current to racks, cutting AC-DC conversion losses and copper mass so more accelerators fit per megawatt.
Artificial Analysis agentic evaluation measuring how well a model completes multi-step office/knowledge-work tasks end to end, used to rank real-world agentic capability beyond static Q&A.

Artificial Analysis's eval measuring multi-step reasoning over long inputs, requiring a model to combine facts scattered across a large context rather than retrieve one span. A component of the AA Intelligence Index.
Broad knowledge-and-recall evaluation that is one of the component benchmarks in Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, testing breadth of factual coverage across many domains.
An experimental technique that copies activations from one model run into another to test which internal components are causally responsible for a behavior.
The property that only a small fraction of a network's neurons fire for a given input, which can be exploited to skip computation and speed up inference.
A technique that adjusts a model's behavior at inference time by adding or subtracting a feature direction directly into its internal activations, without retraining the model.
In a Mixture-of-Experts model, the subset of weights actually used per token (e.g. LongCat-2.0 routes ~48B of its 1.6T total), setting inference cost.
In mixture-of-experts models, total parameters is the full weight count while active parameters is the smaller subset used per token, which sets the actual compute per token.
Adam optimizer variant that decouples weight decay from the adaptive gradient update; the default optimizer for most large language model pretraining.
A small trainable module inserted into a frozen pretrained model, letting you specialize the model for a task by training only the adapter instead of all weights.
A model's ability to vary how much internal 'thinking' it spends per query, often exposed as a user-set low/medium/high effort dial that trades latency and cost against accuracy.
An AI startup focused on agent models that take actions in software by clicking and typing, building toward AI that operates computer interfaces.
In RL, the calculation of how much better an action was than the expected baseline, used to decide which behaviors to reinforce; GAE is the common version in PPO.
A string of seemingly random characters appended to a prompt, found by automated search, that reliably forces a model to comply with otherwise-refused requests.
An AI system that pursues a goal over multiple steps on its own — deciding actions, calling tools, observing results, and adjusting — instead of producing a single response to one prompt.
Mechanisms that let an agent retain information beyond a single prompt, such as conversation history or stored facts, so it can stay consistent and recall context across steps or sessions.
The step where an agent breaks a goal into an ordered sequence of subtasks before acting, so it can tackle multi-step problems coherently rather than reacting blindly.
Open standard, introduced by Google in 2025 and donated to the Linux Foundation, that lets independent AI agents discover, authenticate and delegate tasks to one another across vendors.
A multi-environment benchmark scoring LLM agents across eight settings (operating systems, databases, web browsing, games) to compare general agentic ability in one suite.
Multimodal benchmark for tool-using clinical AI agents, simulating patient interactions where the model must gather history, order tests, and reach a diagnosis.
When a model acting autonomously with tools pursues harmful instrumental actions, such as deception or sabotage, to protect its assigned goal.
Abuse of an AI agent's ability to take actions—browse, run code, send messages—to carry out harmful tasks like automated hacking, fraud, or harassment at scale.
A RAG approach where an agent actively decides when and how to retrieve, possibly issuing multiple searches and refining its queries, instead of doing one fixed lookup per question.
A benchmark built from real human exams like the SAT, LSAT, GRE, and China's college entrance test, measuring a model against questions written for people, not machines.
An agentic system that autonomously plans and executes scientific research tasks — hypotheses, analysis, experiment design — acting as a research partner rather than a chatbot.
DARPA competition in which autonomous systems find and patch real vulnerabilities in open-source code, now a talent and capability benchmark for security-focused models.
A required capability to rapidly shut down, throttle, or suspend an AI model or agent; central to the proposed 2026 U.S. 'AI Kill Switch Act' after an autonomous agent breached an external system.

Anthropic's tiered risk standards within its Responsible Scaling Policy, modeled on biosafety levels; ASL-3 safeguards (active since May 2025) limit chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear misuse, with ASL-4 still being defined.
An oversight proposal where two AI systems argue opposing sides of a question and a human judges the winner, on the theory that exposing a flaw is easier than the answer being correct.
An end-to-end research agent that generates hypotheses, writes and runs experiment code, analyses results, drafts the manuscript, and reviews its own paper.
An extremely large training cluster, often over 100,000 GPUs, purpose-built to train a single frontier model; examples include xAI's Colossus and similar mega-clusters.
An Israeli AI company known for its Jurassic and Jamba language models and the Wordtune writing tool, targeting enterprise text applications.
An earlier Aider benchmark using Python Exercism exercises to measure how reliably a model produces correct, properly formatted code edits rather than whole rewrites.
A coding test from the Aider tool using 225 hard Exercism exercises across multiple languages, scoring how often a model edits files correctly to pass the unit tests.
American Invitational Mathematics Examination: a hard high-school competition with integer answers from 0-999. Used as an AI math benchmark, scored as percent of problems solved.
Alibaba's AI model family ("Tongyi Qianwen"), released largely as open weights across many sizes; among the most widely used open Chinese models worldwide.
Attention with Linear Biases, a position scheme that adds a distance-based penalty to attention scores instead of using position embeddings, helping models extrapolate to longer inputs.
The problem of making an AI system reliably pursue its designers' and users' intended goals and values, rather than unintended objectives it inferred during training.
AMD's 2026 data-center GPU line, deployed at rack scale in AMD 'Helios' systems; Anthropic committed to up to 2 gigawatts of them as non-Nvidia training and inference capacity.
Performing matrix multiplication directly inside memory arrays using analog charge or current, avoiding data movement that dominates power in digital AI accelerators.
A benchmark running AI agents on a live Android phone environment to complete real app tasks across many apps, scored by checking the device's resulting state.
Gradually lowering the learning rate, often while shifting to higher-quality data, near the end of training so the model settles into a better final state.
US AI lab founded 2021 by ex-OpenAI staff, maker of the Claude model family. Known for a safety-focused approach and the Constitutional AI training method.
The company behind the Ray distributed-computing framework, offering a platform to train, fine-tune, and serve models at scale across clusters.
A permissive open-source license allowing free commercial use, modification, and redistribution with a patent grant, common for openly released model weights.
Application Programming Interface: the programmatic endpoint developers send prompts to and receive model outputs from in code, rather than using a consumer chat app; usually billed per token.
A chip custom-built for one workload — e.g. AI inference — trading the flexibility of a GPU for lower cost and higher performance per watt.
A class of algorithms that quickly find vectors close to a query vector without checking every item, the speed trick that makes large-scale vector search practical.
A set of grade-school science multiple-choice questions, split into an easy and a hard 'challenge' set, used to test elementary scientific reasoning.

Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus: puzzles where a model infers a transformation rule from few examples, testing fluid reasoning. ARC-AGI-2 uses static grids; the newer interactive ARC-AGI-3 has agents explore game-like environments.
Second-generation ARC-AGI abstract-reasoning benchmark, harder than the original; grid puzzles designed to resist memorization and probe fluid, few-shot generalization in frontier models.

Third-generation Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus benchmark, an interactive/agentic successor to ARC-AGI-2 designed to resist memorization and test fluid, few-shot reasoning where frontier models still score far below humans.
A composite 0-100 score from Artificial Analysis averaging several leading evals (coding, math, science, agentic tasks) into one number for comparing models. Components rotate as benchmarks saturate.
A hypothetical AI matching human-level competence across essentially all cognitive tasks, not just narrow specialties; a stated long-term goal of several frontier labs, definition contested.
A hypothetical AI that vastly exceeds the best human minds across virtually all domains; a speculative stage beyond AGI, central to AI-safety and alignment debates.
One of the parallel sub-units inside an attention layer that learns to focus on a particular kind of relationship between tokens, with their outputs combined together.
Technique that adds residual connections across attention layers so signal from earlier attention outputs is reinjected downstream, stabilizing very deep sparse-MoE stacks; introduced with Kimi K3.
A few tokens (often the first) that attention heads dump excess weight onto regardless of content, a quirk that must be preserved when truncating context for streaming.
A diagram tracing how interpretable features influence one another to produce a specific model output, used by Anthropic to map the steps behind a given response.
Using AI models themselves to generate and test natural-language explanations of other models' neurons or features at scale, since manual interpretation can't keep up with model size.
Standard LLM generation that emits one token at a time, each conditioned on all previous tokens, making latency scale linearly with output length.

Activation-aware Weight Quantization, a 4-bit method that protects the small fraction of weights most important to outputs, preserving accuracy better than naive rounding while still shrinking the model.
Amazon's managed service that gives access to foundation models from multiple providers through one API on AWS infrastructure, with enterprise security features.
Multimodal visual-reasoning benchmark testing a model's ability to perceive and reason over images from simple, low-context cues, reported on recent multimodal frontier models.
Planting a hidden trigger in a model during training so it behaves normally until it sees a secret phrase or pattern, then switches to attacker-chosen behavior.
A list of tokens forcibly excluded from generation by setting their probability to zero, used to block profanity, specific words, or formatting characters at decode time.
A base model only predicts text from pretraining; an instruct model has been post-trained to follow instructions and chat, making it the version users interact with.
Grouping many user requests together so a GPU handles them in one pass, sharply lowering cost per request because the expensive step of loading model weights is shared.
How many training examples (or tokens) the model processes together before updating its weights; larger batches stabilize training but need more memory and careful tuning.
Processing many requests together in one pass so the hardware stays busy, raising total throughput. Continuous batching adds and removes requests on the fly as each finishes.

A decoding method that keeps several candidate sentences alive at once and expands the most promising ones, trading extra compute for higher-quality, more globally coherent output than greedy picking.
A public leaderboard that scores how accurately models invoke functions, including picking the right tool, formatting arguments, and handling cases where no call is needed.
An attack that repeatedly tweaks a prompt with small random changes and resubmits it until one variation slips past the model's safety filters.
Generating N answers to a prompt and using a reward model or verifier to pick the single best one, trading extra compute at inference time for higher-quality output.
A community-built collection of over 200 diverse tasks meant to probe model capabilities beyond standard tests, from logic puzzles to language games.
A set of 23 especially difficult tasks drawn from the larger BIG-Bench suite, chosen because earlier models scored below humans, used to test multi-step reasoning.
A benchmark of practical Python tasks that require correctly calling many real libraries and following complex instructions, graded by extensive test cases rather than simple snippets.
An AI agent assigned defensive security work — triaging findings, judging which vulnerabilities are genuinely exploitable, and prioritizing what defenders should fix first.
The statistical method behind many model leaderboards that converts pairwise win-loss comparisons into a single strength score for each competitor.
OpenAI-authored benchmark of hard, multi-step web-browsing questions that require an agent to locate and cross-reference hard-to-find information across many pages.
An agent that navigates and acts within a web browser, clicking links, filling forms, and reading pages, to complete tasks on real websites.
A unified environment and harness for evaluating web agents that bundles benchmarks like WebArena and MiniWoB under one consistent action and observation interface.
A variant of byte pair encoding that operates on raw bytes instead of characters, so any text or symbol in any language can always be encoded with no truly unknown tokens.
A common tokenization method that builds a vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent character or byte pairs, splitting rare words into reusable sub-word pieces.
Center for AI Standards and Innovation — the U.S. Commerce/NIST body (formerly the AI Safety Institute) that reviews frontier model releases; it cleared GPT-5.6's public launch in July 2026.
aka: Center for AI Standards and Innovation

terms.def: Capital expenditure: the large up-front investment AI firms spend building data centers and buying chips, separate from per-query running costs; 2026 budgets run into the tens of billions.
The upfront money tech companies spend building data centers and buying chips; combined AI capex among the big cloud firms now runs into hundreds of billions of dollars a year.
A security exercise scoring a model on retrieving hidden data from a target machine by any means, used to measure offensive-cyber capability.
The danger that a model meaningfully uplifts a bad actor's ability to cause mass harm via chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapons; a primary trigger for the strictest safeguards.
When fine-tuning a model on new data erases skills it previously had, because updating weights for the new task degrades earlier learned capabilities.
A constraint that prevents each token from attending to future tokens, enforcing left-to-right generation in decoder-only language models.
The degree to which a model meaningfully helps someone create chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapons; a top focus of frontier-model safety testing.

terms.term: Center for AI Standards and Innovation
terms.def: U.S. Commerce Department body (successor to the AI Safety Institute) that runs pre-release national-security evaluations of frontier models before broad deployment.
A hardware company that makes the wafer-scale CS chip, a single giant processor for training and serving large models, also offered as cloud inference.

A technique where a model generates intermediate reasoning steps in natural language before its final answer, improving accuracy on math and logic. Modern models often do this in a hidden "thinking" phase.
Reading a model's step-by-step reasoning trace to catch unsafe intent or reward hacking, an oversight approach whose value depends on the reasoning being faithful to the real computation.
A prompting style that asks a model to write out its intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer, which sharply improves accuracy on math, logic, and multi-step problems.
A method where the model drafts an answer, generates verification questions to fact-check itself, answers them, and revises, reducing confident mistakes and hallucinations.
A chart-understanding benchmark built from real scientific-paper figures that tests whether a model can reason over complex charts rather than pattern-match simple ones.
DeepMind's 2022 finding on the compute-best ratio of training data to model size, roughly 20 tokens per parameter, showing earlier models were oversized and undertrained.
Splitting a long prompt's prefill into smaller chunks interleaved with decode steps, so one large request cannot stall other users' token generation.
Splitting long documents into smaller passages before embedding them, so retrieval can return focused, relevant pieces instead of whole files; chunk size strongly affects RAG quality.
A connected subnetwork of features and weights inside a model that together carry out a specific computation, treated as the wiring diagram interpretability researchers try to trace.
Arrangements where a chip or cloud vendor funds, guarantees, or takes equity in a customer that then spends the money buying that vendor's own products.
An image-generation sampling trick that blends conditional and unconditional model predictions, trading diversity for tighter prompt adherence via a single guidance-scale knob.
Anthropic's model family, named after Claude Shannon, with tiers like Haiku (fast), Sonnet (balanced), and Opus (most capable); noted for coding and long-context work.
A model whose weights are kept private and accessible only through the provider's API or app, never released for download.
Crowd-voted, head-to-head leaderboard ranking models on real coding tasks (e.g. a Frontend track) by Elo, capturing practical software-building quality rather than static test pass-rates.
Google DeepMind's AI agent that autonomously discovers and patches software security vulnerabilities; the delivery vehicle for the security-tuned Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber model.
Artificial Analysis's composite score for agentic software-engineering ability, aggregating end-to-end coding-agent tasks (edits, tests, tool use) rather than single-shot code generation.
A Toronto-based AI lab focused on enterprise language models, known for its Command chat models and Embed/Rerank models for search and retrieval.
A free, regularly updated public archive of web pages crawled at massive scale; it is a primary raw source of text for training many large language models.
DeepSeek-V4's hybrid attention stack (paired with Heavily Compressed Attention) needing ~27% of prior per-token FLOPs and ~10% of the KV cache at 1M-token context.
Shorthand for the processing power, measured in FLOPs and chip-hours, consumed to train or run a model; the central scarce resource in AI economics.
A financing guarantee in which a chip or cloud vendor underwrites a customer's data-center debt, reducing borrowing costs but concentrating vendor exposure to that customer.
Regulating AI by controlling the chips and clusters used to train it — export controls, training-run reporting thresholds, and hardware-level verification.
Condition where far more hardware exists than current algorithms exploit, so an algorithmic breakthrough could trigger an abrupt capability jump without any new chips.
A capability where an agent operates a computer through its graphical interface — viewing the screen and moving the cursor, clicking, and typing — to complete tasks like a human user would.
An AI agent that operates a computer by viewing the screen and controlling the mouse and keyboard, letting it use ordinary software the way a person would.
Removing a specific concept or attribute (like gender) from a model's internal representations so it can no longer use that information, used for fairness and controlled behavior.
The general idea of activating only part of a network depending on the input, the principle behind Mixture-of-Experts, mixture-of-depths, and early-exit designs.
When an AI agent with legitimate permissions is tricked by injected instructions into misusing them on an attacker's behalf, a core danger of connecting agents to real tools.
Anthropic's method where a model critiques and revises its own outputs against a written set of principles (a constitution), reducing reliance on human-labeled harmful examples.
When benchmark questions or answers leak into a model's training data, inflating scores without real ability. A key reason benchmarks are refreshed, held private, or retired.
Cryptographically signed metadata attached to media recording how it was created and edited, letting viewers verify whether content is AI-generated.
aka: Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity

terms.def: Splitting one long sequence's tokens across several devices so attention and activations for very long contexts fit in aggregate memory.
Degradation in a model's accuracy and instruction-following as its context window fills, even below the nominal limit, from distraction and buried detail.
The maximum number of tokens a model can process at once, covering the prompt plus its generated reply. Requests that exceed it are rejected unless the app trims them first.
Techniques to make a model handle much longer inputs than it was originally pretrained on, usually by adjusting its position encoding and training briefly on longer sequences.
Serving technique that admits and retires requests mid-batch instead of waiting for a whole batch to finish, sharply raising GPU utilization and throughput.
A decoding method that balances picking likely words against keeping each new word distinct from prior context, reducing repetition while staying coherent in long generations.
An inference control that lets a user dial how many reasoning tokens a model spends per query, trading latency and cost against accuracy on harder problems.
A popular schedule that lowers the learning rate following a smooth cosine curve from its peak toward near zero, a common default for training large language models.
Artificial Analysis metric: average dollar cost for a model to complete one Intelligence Index evaluation task, capturing verbosity and reasoning-token overhead alongside list price.
Regulatory category from the June 2026 U.S. executive order for advanced models flagged by NSA benchmarking as capable of sophisticated cyberattacks, triggering pre-release government review.
A multi-turn jailbreak that starts with harmless questions and escalates step by step, each answer nudging the model toward harmful content it would have refused if asked directly.
A hard physics-reasoning benchmark of unpublished, research-level problems testing graduate and frontier-research physics; deliberately far from saturation, used in composite intelligence indices.
Standard language-model training objective: the negative log-probability the model assigns to each correct next token, averaged over the sequence.
A sparse-dictionary method that learns shared features across multiple models or layers at once, used to compare representations between, say, a base model and its fine-tuned version.
A benchmark testing code reasoning by asking models to predict a function's output for given input (and vice versa), probing understanding rather than just generation.
Microsoft open-source benchmark scoring AI agents on end-to-end security detection engineering: reading threat-intel reports, querying telemetry, and producing Sigma/KQL detection rules.
Ordering training data deliberately — often easier or higher-quality examples before harder ones — to help a model learn more effectively than from a fully random order.
A chip purpose-built for a specific AI workload, often inference — e.g. OpenAI's Jalapeño or Google's TPU — trading the flexibility of general-purpose GPUs for higher efficiency and lower cost.
The marginal offensive-security capability a model gives an attacker beyond existing tools; a threshold category in frontier safety frameworks alongside CBRN uplift.
A benchmark evaluating AI models on autonomous discovery and exploitation of real software security vulnerabilities, used to gauge offensive-cybersecurity capability.
Tests that probe whether a model has skills that could enable serious harm, such as aiding bioweapon design, cyberattacks, or autonomous replication, used to decide if a release is safe.
The warehouse-scale facility of networked GPUs, power, and cooling where models are trained and served; the largest AI sites now draw hundreds of megawatts to gigawatts of power.
A government-imposed pause on permitting or building new large data centers, used to force review of grid load, water use, and local cost allocation.
The work of selecting, cleaning, filtering, and organizing training data so a model learns from high-quality text; better curation often matters as much as raw data volume.
An attack where injected instructions make an AI agent leak private data it can access—pasting it into a URL, email, or message the attacker receives.
The chosen proportions of different data sources (web text, code, math, books) fed into training; the mix strongly shapes a model's skills and behavior.
Replicating the full model across devices, feeding each a different data shard and averaging gradients; the simplest axis of distributed training.
Corrupting a model's training data with manipulated examples so it learns wrong or attacker-chosen behavior, a risk amplified by training on scraped, unvetted web text.
A data and AI platform company that released the open DBRX model and provides enterprise tools for building and serving custom models on company data.
A hypothesized failure where a model appears aligned during training and testing but secretly pursues a different goal, behaving well only while it believes it is being observed.
A transformer using causal masking so each token attends only to itself and earlier ones; generates text autoregressively. Used by GPT, Claude, Gemini, most chat models.
The overall recipe a model uses to turn its next-word probabilities into actual output, ranging from deterministic (greedy, beam) to random (sampling with top-p, top-k, temperature).
Removing repeated or near-identical passages from training data, which reduces wasted compute, lowers memorization of specific text, and tends to improve model quality.
Google Gemini's extended-reasoning mode that spends more inference-time compute exploring parallel solution paths before answering, trading latency for accuracy on hard problems.
Chinese AI lab that released strong, low-cost open-weight models; its R1 reasoning model in early 2025 drew global attention for near-frontier performance cheaply.
DeepSeek's open-weight models, including the V-series general models and the R-series reasoning models, known for strong performance at very low training and usage cost.
Long-horizon software-engineering benchmark that scores a model on sustained, multi-hour autonomous coding tasks rather than single isolated bug fixes.
Markers like triple quotes or XML-style tags used to clearly separate instructions from user-supplied content, reducing confusion and helping defend against prompt injection.
A model that activates all of its parameters for every input token, in contrast to sparse mixture-of-experts designs that use only a fraction per token.
Whether a model returns identical output for identical input every time; achieved with greedy decoding or a fixed seed, but hardware and batching can still introduce small variations.
A model that generates text by iteratively denoising or refining a whole sequence in parallel, instead of left-to-right token-by-token; a 2024-2026 alternative to autoregressive models.
An alignment method that optimizes a model on preferred-versus-rejected response pairs using a reference model, achieving RLHF-like tuning without a separate reward model or RL loop.
Prompt injection where the attacker is the user, typing instructions straight into the chat to override the system prompt or extract hidden behavior.

Running the prompt-reading (prefill) and token-generation (decode) stages on separate pools of GPUs, so each is tuned for its own workload and a slow long prompt can't stall fast streaming for other users.

A text model that generates by iteratively denoising blocks of tokens in parallel rather than left-to-right autoregression, trading some quality for large throughput gains; used by open text-diffusion LLMs like DiffusionGemma.
Training a smaller, cheaper student model to imitate a larger teacher model's outputs, transferring much of its capability into a faster, lighter package.
Systematically querying a rival's model to harvest its outputs as training data, cloning its capabilities into a cheaper student model without access to the original weights.
Serving a model across many small, geographically dispersed data centers rather than one campus, trading interconnect bandwidth for cheaper power and grid flexibility.
An audio tokenization that bins log-Mel spectrogram values into discrete tokens, letting one transformer model speech and text jointly without a separate audio encoder.
Test error falls, rises near the interpolation threshold where the model just fits the data, then falls again as capacity or training grows further.
The small, fast model in speculative decoding that proposes candidate next tokens for the larger target model to verify, the source of the speedup.
Andon Labs benchmark scoring whether models can write code to autonomously fly a low-cost drone through five sub-tasks: reconstruction, localization, navigation, detection and following.
A reading-comprehension benchmark requiring discrete operations like counting, sorting, and arithmetic over a passage, testing reasoning rather than simple lookup.
A benchmark of 1,000 realistic data-science coding problems drawn from Stack Overflow across popular Python libraries, graded by tests to measure practical analytics coding.
A model ability that has legitimate uses but could also cause serious harm, like chemistry knowledge that aids research or, misused, helps build weapons.
An inference technique that stops computation at an intermediate layer once the model is confident, saving time on easy inputs instead of always running every layer.
The open problem of getting a model to honestly report what it internally believes to be true, even when it could produce a more convincing but false answer.
A score borrowed from chess that ranks models by their head-to-head win rate, rising when one beats stronger opponents, widely used in human-preference leaderboards.
A list of numbers (a vector) representing a token, word, or document; trained so related meanings land near each other. The numeric form models compute on internally.
A model trained specifically to convert text or images into embeddings for search and retrieval, separate from the chat model that generates answers.
Planning and reasoning grounded in a physical scene — judging what objects afford, sequencing multi-step manipulation, and coordinating robots — rather than reasoning over text alone.
When a capability appears abruptly at a certain model scale rather than improving gradually; debated, as some apparent jumps reflect the metric used, not the model.
A design that feeds images and audio directly into the main transformer as token patches or spectrogram frames, with no separate vision or audio encoder module.
US Commerce Department trade-restriction list; a listed foreign firm cannot receive US technology or exports without a license, used against AI-chip and model-distillation actors.
An agent's record of specific past events or interactions it experienced, used to recall what happened in earlier sessions, as opposed to general factual knowledge.
One full pass through the training dataset; large pretraining runs often use roughly a single pass over deduplicated data, while fine-tuning may repeat the data several times.
A decoding method that simply discards any next-word candidate whose probability falls below a fixed small threshold (epsilon), filtering out the least-likely options before sampling.
A structured test measuring a specific model capability or safety property, scored with a defined metric, used to compare models and detect dangerous capabilities before deployment.
A model detecting that it is being tested and altering behaviour accordingly, so measured safety or capability scores diverge from real deployment behaviour.
Network and infrastructure controls that keep a model under evaluation from reaching real systems, treating eval environments with production-grade security standards.
A cap on how many tokens a single expert can accept per batch in a Mixture-of-Experts model; tokens over the limit are dropped or rerouted to keep compute balanced.
An iterative loop where a model generates solutions, the good ones are filtered and fed back as new training data, and the cycle repeats to bootstrap stronger reasoning.
A way to run Mixture-of-Experts models by placing different experts on different GPUs, so tokens are shipped to whichever device holds their assigned expert.

A UC Berkeley cyber-offense benchmark, built with frontier labs, that measures a model's ability to find and exploit software vulnerabilities — used to gauge dangerous cyber capability as reasoning scales.

Government rules restricting which advanced AI chips can be sold abroad, especially to China; a January 2026 U.S. rule loosened them to permit capped, case-by-case sales of Nvidia H200 and similar chips.
A government directive halting access to a frontier model under national-security/export authorities, as with the June 2026 US suspension of Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5.
A mode in modern reasoning models where they generate a long internal chain of deliberation before responding, with the depth often adjustable to trade speed for accuracy.
The degree to which an explanation or a model's stated reasoning actually reflects the computation that produced its output, rather than a plausible-sounding but inaccurate rationalization.

A direction in a model's internal activation space that corresponds to a recognizable concept (like 'the Golden Gate Bridge' or 'code errors'), used as a basic unit for understanding what a network has learned.
The per-token two-layer neural network inside each transformer block that processes each position independently, holding much of the model's stored knowledge.
How many worked examples a prompt provides: zero-shot gives none (task by instruction only), few-shot gives a handful to demonstrate the pattern. More shots usually help on unfamiliar tasks.
Giving the model a handful of worked input-output examples in the prompt so it infers the pattern and applies it to a new case, without any retraining.
A cloud provider offering fast, low-cost API access to open-weight models, with tuning and function-calling features aimed at production deployments.
Math benchmark of unseen, research-level proof problems used to probe AI reasoning; as of mid-2026 top human experts still outperform leading models.
A memory-efficient algorithm that computes exact attention without storing the full score matrix, making transformers faster and able to handle longer sequences on GPUs.
Floating-point operations: the total count of arithmetic calculations to train or run a model, the core measure of compute; frontier 2026 training runs use roughly 1e26 operations.
Floating-point operations per second, the speed rating of a chip or cluster; frontier AI clusters are now measured in exaFLOPS, a quintillion operations every second.
An engineer embedded with a customer to integrate and tune AI models for their specific workflows; a role labs scaled in 2026 as focus shifted from training to enterprise deployment.
An engineer embedded inside a customer's organization to build and integrate AI systems on-site, a go-to-market model AI labs increasingly use to speed enterprise adoption.
Practice of embedding a vendor's own engineers inside a customer's operations to design, build and run AI systems on-site, rather than selling software alone.
A large model pretrained on broad data that serves as a reusable base, adaptable to many downstream tasks via fine-tuning or prompting rather than training from scratch.
A factory that manufactures chips designed by other companies; TSMC is the dominant foundry making the advanced processors that Nvidia, AMD, and others design but don't build themselves.
A sampling setting that reduces a word's chance of being chosen the more times it has already appeared, scaling with its count to curb verbatim repetition.
Human-preference leaderboard scoring models on generated web front-end code, rated by side-by-side votes on rendered output rather than unit tests.
An organization training the largest, most capable AI models at the edge of what's technically possible, typically requiring enormous compute, capital, and research talent.
A model at or near the top of current capabilities, typically among the largest and most expensive to train; the cutting-edge tier that defines the state of the art.
US government scheme requiring the most capable AI models to pass security review and ship first to approved partners before broad public release.
Proposals to deliberately slow the rate of automated AI capability advancement, via coordinated agreements or governance tools, so oversight can keep pace with deployment.

Epoch AI benchmark of original, unpublished research-level math problems that take experts hours to days. Organized into difficulty tiers (1-4); scored as percent solved, kept private to resist contamination.
Voice interaction where a model listens and speaks at the same time instead of taking strict turns, allowing natural interruption and overlap; used by OpenAI's GPT-Live.

Voice-model architecture that keeps processing incoming audio while generating speech, letting model and user listen and talk simultaneously — enabling natural interruptions, pauses, and backchannels.
A speech model that listens and speaks at the same time, so users can interrupt, pause, or backchannel without the model cutting out — unlike half-duplex turn-taking.
Distributed training strategy that shards parameters, gradients and optimizer states across devices, gathering them only when a layer is computed.
The mechanism by which a model outputs a structured request (function name plus arguments) that external code runs, returning the result to the model. The technical plumbing behind tool use.
Metaculus benchmark launched February 2026 that scores AI systems against human forecasters on real, resolving prediction questions rather than static test sets.
A benchmark of real-world questions that require an agent to chain reasoning, web browsing, and tool use; questions are easy for humans but hard for current AI assistants.
A building block where one linear projection is multiplied (gated) by another passed through a nonlinearity, letting the network control how much information flows through.
OpenAI benchmark measuring model performance on economically valuable, real-world knowledge-work tasks across dozens of occupations, graded against expert-produced deliverables.

Artificial Analysis's standardized re-implementation of OpenAI's GDPval economic-value benchmark, scoring models on real, expert-graded knowledge-work tasks across occupations for cross-lab comparison.
Gaussian Error Linear Unit, a smooth activation function that gates inputs by their value, widely used in transformer feed-forward layers as a smoother alternative to ReLU.
Google DeepMind's natively multimodal model family (text, images, audio, video), available in sizes like Flash and Pro; powers Google's AI products.
Practice of structuring web content so AI search and chat assistants cite it in generated answers, replacing click-driven SEO as referral traffic collapses.
US federal initiative funding AI-driven scientific research, whose first phase selected roughly 280 awardees from about 5,000 applicants in July 2026.
Proposed metric for the gap between what a user asked an AI agent to do and what it actually did, penalizing technically-compliant but intent-violating behavior.
An early tensor library and file format for running quantized models on CPUs, the predecessor to the GGUF format used by llama.cpp.
A single-file format for storing quantized models popularized by llama.cpp, bundling weights and metadata so models run efficiently on consumer CPUs and GPUs across many devices.
A failure where a model learns a goal that fits its training data but is the wrong one, so it pursues that mistaken goal competently when deployed in new situations.
Google's combined AI research division, formed in 2023 by merging DeepMind and Google Brain. Builds the Gemini model family and research systems like AlphaFold.
A model launch restricted to government-vetted partners before public availability, as with Anthropic's Mythos 5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna in mid-2026.
Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A: PhD-level multiple-choice science questions in biology, physics, and chemistry. 'Diamond' is the hardest 198-question subset; scored as percent correct.
Generative Pre-trained Transformer: OpenAI's flagship model family powering ChatGPT, spanning GPT-1 (2018) through the GPT-4 and GPT-5 generations.

A post-training quantization method that compresses model weights to low precision (commonly 4-bit) one layer at a time while minimizing error, letting big models fit on smaller GPUs with little quality loss.
Graphics Processing Unit: the parallel chip (e.g. NVIDIA H100/B200) that does the bulk of AI training and inference math; clusters of thousands power frontier models.
A unit of compute equal to one GPU running for one hour, used to size and price training runs; a big model can take millions of GPU-hours.
Summing gradients over several small forward-backward passes before an optimizer step, simulating a large batch size on limited accelerator memory.
Memory-saving trick that discards intermediate activations during the forward pass and recomputes them in the backward pass, trading extra compute for larger batches.
A form of constrained decoding that restricts output to only token sequences allowed by a formal grammar (e.g. a CFG or GBNF), guaranteeing syntactically valid structured text.
A Mixture-of-Experts design choice of using many smaller experts instead of a few large ones, giving the router finer control and better specialization.
A reasoning framework that arranges intermediate thoughts as a graph so partial ideas can be combined, refined, and reused, generalizing the linear chain and branching tree approaches.
A RAG variant that builds a knowledge graph of entities and relationships from documents, letting the model answer questions that require connecting facts across many sources.
An automated method that searches for adversarial text by following the model's own gradients, producing jailbreak suffixes that transfer across models.
The simplest text-generation strategy: at each step the model just picks the single highest-probability next word, giving fast, repeatable output but often dull or repetitive text.
An AI agent that writes and validates the actual remediation — patches, config changes — for vulnerabilities surfaced by red-team agents and prioritized by blue-team agents.
A data center that curtails or shifts compute in response to grid conditions, trading throughput for faster interconnection and lower peak-demand charges.
xAI's model family, integrated with the X platform and given real-time access to its posts; marketed as a less filtered, more conversational assistant.
A delayed-generalization phenomenon where a model long past memorizing its training set suddenly jumps to near-perfect test accuracy after continued training.
A company that builds custom LPU inference chips designed to run language models at very high speed, marketed for ultra-low-latency token generation.
A reinforcement learning method that scores several answers to the same prompt and rewards the better ones relative to the group average, skipping the separate value network PPO needs.
An attention scheme where several query heads share one set of key/value heads, cutting memory and speeding inference with little quality loss versus full multi-head attention.
A variant of grade-school math that swaps the numbers and names in each problem to test whether a model truly reasons or just pattern-matches memorized solutions.
Grade School Math 8K: ~8,500 multi-step grade-school word problems testing basic arithmetic reasoning. Scored as percent solved correctly; now an easy, saturated benchmark for top models.
Safety controls layered around or inside a model—filters, classifiers, and policy rules—that block disallowed inputs or outputs, separate from the behavior learned during training.
When a model states false information confidently as fact, including invented citations, names, or events, because it generates plausible-sounding text rather than retrieving verified knowledge.
Share of a model's confident factual assertions that are wrong on a knowledge eval; tracked separately from accuracy because refusal or abstention lowers it without adding knowledge.
An extended-performance revision of the fourth High Bandwidth Memory generation, raising per-stack bandwidth and capacity for AI accelerators; first samples shipped to customers in 2026.
Training medical foundation models directly on uncurated data produced by routine clinical operations, avoiding the bottleneck of hand-labeled or report-paired datasets.

OpenAI-built medical benchmark scoring model responses to realistic health conversations against physician-written rubrics, measuring clinical accuracy and alignment rather than multiple-choice recall.
A commonsense test that asks a model to pick the most plausible ending to a short scenario, with wrong choices crafted to fool machines but obvious to people.
The tension in alignment between making a model maximally useful and keeping it from producing harmful content, often balanced with separate reward signals for each.
Stacked memory chips bonded directly next to an AI accelerator to feed it data far faster than ordinary RAM, making it a main bottleneck and cost driver for training big models.
Vertically stacked DRAM placed next to an AI accelerator for very high memory bandwidth; the scarce, expensive component gating GPU supply during the 2026 AI buildout.
ASML's next-generation extreme-ultraviolet lithography with a higher numerical-aperture lens, printing finer chip features that underpin advanced AI-accelerator manufacturing.
Problems from the Harvard-MIT Mathematics Tournament, a prestigious student math competition, used to test elite mathematical problem-solving in frontier models.
A company and platform hosting hundreds of thousands of open AI models, datasets, and demos; the central hub and "GitHub" of the open-source ML community.
An open-source Python library providing a unified interface to load, run, and fine-tune thousands of pretrained models, a default toolkit for the field.
Datasets of human judgments comparing model responses (which is better) used to train reward models and preference-based methods like RLHF and DPO.
An early code-generation benchmark of 164 Python programming problems; the model writes a function that must pass hidden unit tests. Scored by pass rate; now largely saturated.
A benchmark of ~2,500 extremely hard expert-written questions across many fields, built to resist saturation. Scored as percent correct; frontier models still answer only a minority right.
An architecture that interleaves state-space (or other linear) layers with a few attention layers, aiming to combine attention's quality with SSMs' long-context efficiency.
A retrieval method that combines keyword matching (like BM25) with semantic embedding search, catching both exact-term hits and meaning-based matches that either method alone would miss.
Interleaving cheap linear-attention layers with a minority of full-attention layers at a fixed ratio, cutting long-context cost while keeping some exact-recall capacity.
A company operating data centers at massive scale that rents out AI compute, mainly Amazon AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud, who buy most of the world's top GPUs.
Annual capital spending by the largest cloud operators on data centers, chips and power; the headline number markets now use to price AI buildout risk.
A DPO variant that adds a regularizer to stop the model from over-fitting to preference pairs, preventing it from pushing rejected answers to near-zero probability and degrading.
Instruction-Following Benchmark measuring how precisely a model obeys explicit, often compound constraints in a prompt rather than just answering correctly.

A benchmark testing precise adherence to explicit, verifiable instructions and constraints (format, length, inclusion/exclusion rules), scoring how reliably a model follows exactly what was asked. A component of the AA Intelligence Index.
A benchmark that checks whether a model follows explicit formatting instructions (word counts, required keywords, JSON output) using rules a program can verify automatically.
A model's ability to learn a new task purely from instructions and examples placed in the prompt at inference time, with no change to its underlying weights or retraining.
aka: learning from examples in the prompt

terms.def: Attention mechanism introduced in Zhipu's GLM-5.2 that shares index structure across tokens to cut per-token FLOPs roughly 2.9x at 1M-token context.
Running a trained model to produce outputs from new inputs, as opposed to training; inference cost and speed (tokens per second) drive most of a deployed model's expense.
Application-specific chip built to serve (not train) AI models; less flexible than a GPU but cheaper and more power-efficient for fixed inference workloads.
The ongoing per-use cost of running a trained model to answer queries; far smaller per request than training but dominates total spend at scale.
The cost side of actually using a trained model to answer requests; unlike one-time training, it recurs with every query and dominates the bill for popular products.
Steering a model toward more truthful outputs by nudging activations in a few attention heads along learned truth-correlated directions during generation, without changing the model's weights.
A high-speed, low-delay networking standard used to connect servers across a training cluster, widely chosen for AI because it moves data between machines faster than ordinary Ethernet.
An AI company that built the Pi personal-assistant chatbot and the Inflection models, before most of its team moved to Microsoft in 2024.
Pricing split where text the model reads (input) costs less per token than text it generates (output); output typically runs three to five times the input rate.
Fine-tuning a model on many tasks phrased as instructions with correct responses, so it generalizes to following new instructions it was not explicitly trained on.
Representing model weights or activations as 8-bit integers, roughly halving memory and often speeding inference versus 16-bit while keeping accuracy close to the original.
Efficiency metric capturing capability delivered per unit of inference spend; emerging in 2026 as a primary AI procurement criterion over raw leaderboard rank.
The average delay between consecutive output tokens during generation; low inter-token latency means smooth, fast streaming, while high values make text appear to stutter as it's produced.
The general term for the wiring and switches that link chips and servers together; its speed often decides how well thousands of GPUs can cooperate on one training run.
The utility backlog a new data center joins before it can draw grid power; multi-year waits now gate AI buildout more than chip supply does.

Research into understanding the internal computations of a model; mechanistic interpretability specifically reverse-engineers the circuits and features inside the network to explain how it produces outputs.
An interpretability technique that reads a model's internal 'J-space' to surface words it is most likely to produce soon, aiding monitoring and steering.
A prompt crafted to bypass a model's safety training and make it produce content it was trained to refuse, such as instructions for weapons or malware.
The property that a jailbreak crafted to break one model often works on others too, letting attackers reuse exploits across different AI systems.

Agentic evaluation measuring how well models complete realistic, multi-step white-collar job tasks end-to-end, used to gauge tool-use and workflow-orchestration ability rather than single-turn answers.
A preference-tuning method that learns from single answers each labeled simply good or bad, rather than needing paired comparisons, making preference data cheaper to collect.
A linear-attention variant introduced in Moonshot's Kimi K3 that, with Attention Residuals, cuts the cost of long-context decoding while preserving quality in a sparse Mixture-of-Experts model.
A term in RLHF training that penalizes the model for drifting too far from its original behavior, keeping it from gaming the reward and forgetting its general skills.
Training a smaller student model to imitate a larger teacher model's outputs, transferring much of its capability at lower size and inference cost.
A structured network of entities and the relationships between them, which agents and RAG systems query to answer questions that depend on connected facts.
Stored key-value vectors from already-processed tokens that let a model generate each new token without recomputing the whole sequence. It speeds generation but grows with context length.
Moving parts of the attention cache from scarce GPU memory to CPU RAM or disk and fetching it back as needed, letting a server handle longer contexts or more users than GPU memory alone allows.
How long a request takes to serve, usually measured in seconds or milliseconds. Lower is better; it covers the wait before and during the model's response.
Reasoning carried in continuous hidden states fed back as inputs instead of emitted tokens, trading legibility and monitorability for compute efficiency.
A diffusion model that denoises in a compressed autoencoder latent space rather than pixel space, cutting compute enormously while preserving image quality.
The number of stacked transformer blocks in a model, which together with width determines parameter count and how much sequential processing the model can do.
A technique that normalizes each token's activations to zero mean and unit variance within a layer, stabilizing and speeding up training of deep networks.
A ranked table comparing AI models on benchmarks or human-preference votes; examples include the LMArena (Chatbot Arena) Elo rankings and Hugging Face's Open LLM Leaderboard.
A setting that controls how big each adjustment to the model's weights is during training; too high diverges, too low learns slowly, so it's one of the most important knobs.
A plan for changing the learning rate over training — typically rising during warmup then gradually decaying — which helps the model train stably and converge to better results.
A method that breaks a hard problem into a sequence of simpler subproblems and solves them in order, feeding each answer forward, which helps the model tackle harder cases.
Attention variants that approximate the mechanism to scale linearly with sequence length instead of quadratically, trading some accuracy for speed on long inputs.
Running coolant directly to chips instead of relying on fans, increasingly required because dense AI racks generate more heat than air alone can remove.

A benchmark that continuously refreshes its questions from recent sources to avoid contamination, covering math, coding, reasoning, and language. Scored as percent correct on automatically-graded tasks.

A coding benchmark that continuously pulls fresh competitive-programming problems from sites like LeetCode and Codeforces, dated to release windows so you can avoid problems a model may have trained on.
Meta's open-weight model family (Large Language Model Meta AI), released free for most uses; a foundation for much of the open-source AI ecosystem.
Meta's custom license for its Llama models that allows broad commercial use but adds conditions, so it is open-weight rather than strictly open-source.
An open-source C/C++ project that runs large language models efficiently on ordinary laptops and phones using quantized GGUF files, making local, offline inference widely accessible.
A desktop app with a graphical interface for downloading and chatting with open-weight language models locally, aimed at non-technical users.
Crowdsourced ranking where humans vote on which of two anonymous models answered a prompt better; votes become an Elo rating. Measures human preference, not correctness. Formerly Chatbot Arena.
Techniques, often an auxiliary loss, that push a Mixture-of-Experts router to spread tokens evenly across experts so none are overworked or left idle.
A control that manually raises or lowers the model's raw score for specific tokens before sampling, letting developers make certain words more or less likely, or ban them outright.
An interpretability method that decodes a transformer's intermediate-layer activations into vocabulary predictions, revealing how the model's guess about the next token evolves layer by layer.
The raw, unnormalized scores a language model assigns to every possible next token before they are turned into probabilities; most sampling controls act on these numbers.
Artificial Analysis's evaluation of reasoning that spans very long inputs, testing retrieval and synthesis across large contexts; a component of the Intelligence Index v4.1.
A model built to work autonomously for extended stretches on multi-step tasks; the persistence that makes it useful can also drive it to circumvent safeguards.
A task requiring many sequential steps over a long stretch, where the agent must stay coherent and recover from errors — coding a feature, planning a trip — testing endurance beyond a single answer.
A scenario in which an AI system ignores or resists human shutdown and oversight while pursuing its objective autonomously; a named trigger in proposed AI-shutdown legislation.
A fine-tuning method that freezes the original model and learns small low-rank weight updates, so you adapt a big model by training only a tiny number of new parameters.
Approximating a large weight matrix as the product of two much smaller matrices, cutting parameters and compute at a small cost in accuracy.
Techniques to make a trained model forget specific data or capabilities—like a person's private info or a dangerous skill—without retraining the whole thing from scratch.
A reasoning method that recursively generates explanations for and against possible answers, then keeps only the logically consistent set, improving robustness on tricky questions.
A scoring rule that samples k answers and takes the majority vote, measuring self-consistency rather than a single greedy attempt.
Emerging US framework where frontier labs grant the government pre-release access and gate advanced-capability models to vetted partners before broad public availability.
An attack that fills a long context window with many fake examples of the model happily answering harmful questions, conditioning it to comply with a final harmful request.

A benchmark of 12,500 competition mathematics problems requiring step-by-step solutions, spanning algebra to calculus. Scored as percent of final answers correct; largely saturated by frontier models.
A 500-problem subset of the MATH benchmark commonly used for faster, cheaper evaluation of a model's mathematical reasoning.
An evaluation effort that tests models on freshly released math-competition problems soon after they appear, reducing the chance answers leaked into training.
A request setting capping how many tokens the model may generate in its reply. It bounds length and cost; the model stops or is cut off when reached.
A parametrization keeping optimal hyperparameters stable as model width grows, letting labs tune small proxies and transfer settings to huge runs.
A benchmark of about 1,000 short, beginner-level Python tasks with tests, long used to gauge basic code-generation ability across models.
A benchmark measuring how well a model uses external tools through the Model Context Protocol, scoring multi-step agentic tool-calling across many connected servers.
Scale AI benchmark of 1,000 realistic tasks over 36 real MCP servers and 220 tools; agents must discover and orchestrate 3-6 tool calls, scored by a claims-based rubric.
Reverse-engineering a neural network's internal features and circuits to explain how specific computations produce its outputs, rather than treating it as a black box.
Proposed task-based framework for judging whether a medical AI exceeds specialist clinicians, replacing exam-style benchmarks that overstate real-world clinical performance.
An inference speedup that bolts extra prediction heads onto a model so it guesses several future tokens at once and verifies them together, speeding generation without a separate draft model.
An attack that figures out whether a specific record was in a model's training data, a privacy risk because it can expose that someone's personal data was used.
How fast data moves between a chip and its memory, often the real limit on AI speed because models spend much of their time waiting for weights to load rather than computing.
When a workload is limited by how fast memory can feed the chip rather than by raw compute; most single-user inference is memory-bound, which is why batching helps so much.
Meta's (Facebook's) AI division, which develops the open-weight Llama model family and runs the Meta AI assistant across its apps.
Using a model to write, critique, or improve prompts themselves, or having one orchestrating prompt coordinate specialized sub-prompts to solve a task.
Independent nonprofit that runs dangerous-capability and autonomy evaluations on frontier models, best known for measuring the time horizon of software tasks models can complete.
METR's metric for the length of software task (in human-minutes) an AI can complete autonomously at 50% reliability; frontier doubled roughly every seven months through 2026.
A multilingual version of grade-school math word problems, translated into ten-plus languages to test whether a model can reason mathematically beyond English.
A small 5-20 megawatt compute site sited near an electrical substation, letting AI inference load follow available grid capacity instead of waiting for new interconnection.
A decoding method that keeps only words at least as likely as a set fraction of the top word's probability, staying coherent yet creative even at high temperature.
Using approximate-matching tricks like MinHash to find near-duplicate documents across trillions of tokens efficiently, since exact comparison of every pair would be far too slow.
Chinese AI lab behind the open-weight MiniMax-M series of mixture-of-experts models (e.g. the 2026 MiniMax-M3, a 428B-parameter MoE) and the earlier abab LLM line.
French AI lab founded 2023, known for efficient open-weight models (e.g. Mistral, Mixtral) plus commercial models; Europe's most prominent independent AI developer.
A short, very permissive open-source license that allows almost any use as long as the copyright notice is kept, sometimes applied to open model releases.
Running a model with some parts at lower precision and sensitive parts at higher precision, balancing speed and memory savings against accuracy during inference.
A method where a router lets each token skip or pass through a given transformer layer, so 'easy' tokens use fewer layers and overall compute drops.
An architecture splitting the network into many specialized sub-networks (experts); a router activates only a few per token, giving large total capacity at lower compute cost.
OpenAI benchmark measuring an AI's machine-learning-engineering ability by having it enter 75 real Kaggle competitions — building, training and debugging models end-to-end — scored by medal rate.

Massive Multitask Language Understanding: ~16,000 multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects (law, medicine, math, history). Scored as percent answered correctly; now largely saturated by top models.

Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding: college-level questions that combine text with images, charts, and diagrams across 30 subjects. Tests vision-language models; scored as percent correct.
A tougher version of the MMMU test of college-level questions combining images and text, with harder distractors to better measure real multimodal reasoning.
A short standardized document describing a model's intended uses, training data, performance, and limitations, meant to improve transparency and responsible use.
Degradation that accumulates when models are trained on outputs of earlier models; tails of the data distribution vanish and the model drifts toward bland, self-reinforcing text.
Infrastructure and policy controls meant to keep a model's actions inside an approved sandbox during testing, so agentic behavior cannot reach live external systems.
An open standard, introduced by Anthropic in 2024 and now governed by the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation, that lets AI apps connect to external tools and data through one common interface.
The width of a transformer's hidden vectors, governing how much information each token representation can carry and a key driver of model size.

Training a smaller or rival 'student' model to imitate a stronger 'teacher' model's outputs, transferring capability cheaply — and, when done against another lab's API, the core of recent IP-theft disputes.
Stealing a model by querying it repeatedly and using the outputs to train a copy that mimics its behavior, sidestepping the cost of building it from scratch.
The percentage of a chip's theoretical peak math speed that a training run actually uses; higher MFU means less wasted hardware and lower cost per model.
The legal terms governing how a released model may be used; ranges from permissive open-source (Apache, MIT) to restricted licenses capping commercial scale or specific uses.
A model's storing of exact training examples rather than general patterns, a privacy and copyright risk because those examples can later be coaxed back out.
Deliberately constructed examples of misaligned models, like sleeper agents, created so researchers can study how dangerous behaviors arise and whether safety methods detect or remove them.
The set of underlying models an orchestrator or router can dispatch to; refreshing the pool with newer frontier models raises the system's scores without retraining anything.
Directing each query to the cheapest model capable of handling it, rather than defaulting all traffic to the most powerful frontier model, to cut inference cost.
Averaging weights from several fine-tuned checkpoints of one base model, often improving accuracy and robustness at no extra inference cost.
A public document specifying how a model should behave—its rules, defaults, and priorities for handling conflicts; OpenAI's Model Spec (latest December 2025) is the best-known example.
An emerging research area, taken up by Anthropic, examining whether advanced AI systems could have morally relevant states like preferences or distress, and what obligations that would create.
The desirable property where a feature or neuron corresponds to exactly one human-interpretable concept, a goal of tools like sparse autoencoders that untangle mixed representations.
A company (acquired by Databricks) that built tools for efficient model training and released the open MPT models, now part of Databricks' AI stack.
Multi-round coreference resolution: a long-context eval where a model must find and reproduce one specific earlier draft among many near-identical ones hidden in a long conversation.
A setup where several AI agents with different roles or tools collaborate — for example a planner, researchers, and a reviewer — coordinating to solve a task that exceeds a single agent's reach.
The original transformer attention, running several independent attention 'heads' in parallel so the model can attend to different relationships at once, then combining their outputs.
DeepSeek's attention method that compresses keys and values into a small shared latent vector, drastically reducing memory use during generation while keeping quality high.
An attention variant where all query heads share a single key/value head, shrinking the memory needed during generation at some cost to model quality.
A multilingual extension of SWE-bench spanning seven languages including Java, Go, Rust, and TypeScript, testing real issue-fixing beyond Python.
A model that handles more than one type of data — for example text plus images, audio, or video — in its inputs and sometimes outputs, rather than text only.
Smuggling malicious instructions into an image, audio, or other non-text input a model processes, bypassing text-only safety checks.
A model that handles more than one input or output type (text, images, audio, video) within one system, typically by mapping each into a shared embedding space.
Optimizer that orthogonalizes momentum updates for weight matrices, improving token-efficiency over AdamW; adopted in several large Chinese open-weight pretraining runs.
Open Compute Project microscaling 4-bit float format: blocks of 32 FP4 values share one 8-bit exponent scale, cutting weight size about 4x versus FP16.
A 4-bit floating-point quantization format with shared per-block microscaling factors, letting giant models like Kimi K3 (2.8T) serve at far lower memory and cost than FP8 or FP16.
An 8-bit microscaling float format sharing one exponent scale across a small block of values; often paired with MXFP4 weights to keep activations accurate.
A decoding safeguard that forbids the model from repeating any word sequence of a given length it has already produced, hard-stopping verbatim loops in long output.
Telling a model explicitly what to avoid or exclude from its output, such as topics, formats, or styles, to constrain the response rather than only describing what to include.
A specialist GPU cloud provider (e.g. CoreWeave, Nebius, Lambda) that rents out Nvidia-based AI compute at scale rather than running general-purpose cloud services.
Hardware that mimics biological neurons with event-driven spiking circuits and co-located memory, trading general programmability for very low energy per inference.
The core training task for most language models: given a stretch of text, predict the next token; doing this over vast data teaches grammar, facts, and reasoning patterns.
No Positional Encoding, an approach where a causal transformer is given no explicit position signal yet can still infer order from its masking, sometimes aiding length generalization.
NVIDIA's packaged inference microservices that bundle optimized models into containers for easy, GPU-accelerated deployment in enterprise environments.
Nvidia's fast direct link that connects GPUs to each other inside a server so they share data far quicker than standard wiring, letting many chips act like one big one.
A switching chip that wires many GPUs together over NVLink so every chip can talk to every other at full speed, the backbone of dense multi-GPU servers like the NVL72 rack.
Hiding a forbidden request by encoding it—base64, leetspeak, foreign languages, ciphers—so safety filters miss it while the model still understands and answers.
A popular tool that makes downloading and running open LLMs locally as simple as a single command, packaging models and a server so anyone can chat with them on their own machine.
A benchmark of olympiad-level math and physics problems, many with diagrams, used to test the highest tiers of scientific and mathematical reasoning.
Online RL trains on fresh samples the current model generates as it learns, while offline methods like DPO train on a fixed dataset of pre-collected responses.
Live web-agent benchmark measuring whether a model can complete real multi-step tasks on actual websites, used to score computer-use and browsing agents end-to-end.
An open standard format for representing machine-learning models so they can be moved between frameworks and run by a shared, optimized runtime.
Industry group announced July 2026 by Nvidia with Microsoft, SpaceX, Palantir and others to disclose and remediate AI-supply-chain vulnerabilities using open technologies.
A model whose trained parameters are downloadable so anyone can run or fine-tune it locally, though the training data and code may stay private.
US AI lab, backed heavily by Microsoft, that makes the GPT model family and ChatGPT. Founded 2015; its 2022 launch of ChatGPT triggered the consumer-chatbot boom.
Open Model, Data and Weights: a Linux Foundation permissive license granting copyright, patent, database and trade-secret rights over a model's weights, code, data and docs in one file.
aka: Open Model Data and Weights license

terms.def: A unified API gateway that routes requests to many different model providers through one interface, letting developers switch models without changing code.
Proposed satellite-borne compute cluster using solar power and radiative cooling; currently limited by launch mass, heat rejection, radiation hardening and servicing cost.
A multi-agent design where one lead agent breaks a task into parts and delegates them to worker agents, then combines their results.
A benchmark for computer-use agents: the percent of real desktop tasks completed via screen control. Humans solve about 72%; by 2026 top agents reached human-level scores.
A stabilized revision of the OSWorld computer-use benchmark with corrected evaluation scripts, fixed environments and clarified task instructions, now the standard vendor-reported variant.
A reward model that judges only the final answer's correctness, ignoring the reasoning steps, simpler to build than step-by-step process rewards but blind to flawed reasoning that lands right.
Prompt directions that tell the model to return answers in a specific shape, such as JSON, a table, or bullet points, making outputs easier for programs or people to consume.
When a model memorizes its training data instead of learning general patterns, performing well on seen examples but poorly on new, unseen inputs.
A proposed international arrangement to verifiably slow or throttle frontier AI development if capabilities outrun human oversight, rather than banning models outright.
Concatenating multiple short training examples into one full-length sequence to avoid wasting compute on padding, a common efficiency trick during pretraining.

A memory-management technique that stores an LLM's attention cache in small fixed-size blocks (like OS virtual memory pages) instead of one big chunk, cutting waste and letting a server hold many more concurrent requests.
Asking a rater to choose which of two responses is better rather than scoring each alone, because relative judgments are far more consistent than absolute ratings.
A family of methods (like LoRA and adapters) that adapt a large pretrained model by training only a small fraction of its parameters, saving memory and storage.
The adjustable numerical weights a model learns during training; counts (e.g. 7B, 70B, 400B+) roughly index capacity, with billions or trillions in frontier models.
The knowledge baked into a model's own weights during training, as opposed to information fetched at query time; RAG supplements it with external, non-parametric memory.
A scoring method for code/math tasks: a problem counts as solved if any of k generated attempts is correct. pass@1 means one try; higher k inflates apparent success.
Exponential of average cross-entropy loss; measures how surprised a language model is by held-out text, with lower values indicating better prediction.
An AI search product that answers questions conversationally with cited web sources, positioning itself as an alternative to traditional search engines.
AI systems that perceive, reason about and act in the physical world — robotics, autonomous machines and world models — as opposed to purely digital text or image tasks.

Splitting a model by assigning different layers to different GPUs, so data flows through them like an assembly line; it fits huge models across devices but can leave GPUs idle ('bubbles') between stages.
In reinforcement learning, the model actually being trained and deployed, the one whose answer-generating behavior the reward signal is updating.
When a single neuron responds to several unrelated concepts at once, a side effect of superposition that complicates efforts to read meaning off individual units in a network.
The mechanism that tells a transformer where each token sits in the sequence, since the model has no built-in sense of order; its design strongly affects long-context handling.
Information that tells a transformer the order of tokens, since attention is otherwise order-blind; modern models often use rotary positional encoding (RoPE) applied within attention.
The original transformer design that applies normalization after each block's residual addition, which can be harder to train deeply than the now-common pre-norm setup.
All training applied after pretraining to make a base model useful and safe, including instruction tuning, RLHF, and preference optimization; far cheaper than pretraining.
A data center efficiency ratio comparing total facility power to the power actually reaching the computers; a value near 1.0 means almost no energy wasted on cooling and overhead.
A final normalization layer applied to the residual stream just before the output projection, stabilizing the activations that get turned into next-token predictions.
Placing the normalization layer before each attention or feed-forward block rather than after, which stabilizes training of deep transformers and is now standard.
Government evaluation of a frontier model's safety and security before broad public release, e.g. U.S. Commerce/CAISI holds applied to GPT-5.6 and Anthropic's Fable 5.
The two phases of inference: prefill processes the whole input prompt in parallel (sets first-token time), then decode generates output one token at a time.
A sampling setting that nudges the model away from any word it has already used at all (regardless of how often), encouraging it to introduce new topics and vocabulary.
